paragraphs.heading: What a curved mirror is
paragraphs.text: A curved mirror has a reflecting surface that is curved, either convex, bulging outward, or concave, recessed inward. Most are shaped like part of a sphere, the simplest shape to make and the best for general use. Some optical devices use other shapes, most often parabolic reflectors, as in reflecting telescopes that image distant objects. They are chosen because spherical mirrors, like spherical lenses, suffer from spherical aberration.

paragraphs.heading: Convex mirrors
paragraphs.text: A convex, or diverging, mirror bulges toward the light source. It reflects light outward, so a parallel beam spreads apart after hitting it, and it is not used to focus light. Its focal point and center of curvature are imaginary points inside the mirror that cannot be reached, so its image is always virtual and cannot be projected onto a screen. Virtual means the rays never actually pass through the image; only their extensions do. The image is also upright and smaller than the object.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing more at a glance
paragraphs.text: As an object nears a convex mirror its image grows, until it is about the object's size at contact; as it moves away, the image shrinks toward a point at the focus. Because everything looks smaller, the mirror covers a wider view than a flat mirror. A car's passenger-side mirror is usually convex, and in some countries it carries the warning Objects in mirror are closer than they appear. Such mirrors also keep watch in shops, parking lots, hallway corners, blind road bends and some cash machines.

paragraphs.heading: The sorcerer's eye
paragraphs.text: From the 15th century, round convex mirrors known as Oeil de Sorcière, which is French for sorcerer's eye, were a popular luxury. With the methods of that century, a curved mirror of blown glass was easier to produce than a perfectly flat one. Their wide view made them handy for security, which earned them the name bankers' eyes. They appear in famous paintings such as the Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck.

paragraphs.heading: Concave mirrors
paragraphs.text: A concave, or converging, mirror is recessed away from the incoming light. It gathers light, reflecting parallel incoming rays inward toward one focal point. This works because the surface faces a different way at each spot, so light reflects at different angles across it. Unlike a convex mirror, the kind of image it shows depends on how far the object is from it.

paragraphs.heading: Where concave mirrors work
paragraphs.text: Reflecting telescopes use concave mirrors, and so do mirrors that magnify the face for make-up or shaving, and some dental mirrors. Torches, headlamps and spotlights use them to gather light from a small source and send it out as a beam. Concentrated solar power uses them the other way, collecting light from a wide area into a small spot. They also form the optical cavities used to build lasers, and the landing aid on modern aircraft carriers.
